description: Width tiers for Digital Technologies Foundation (ACARA v9). One entry per descriptor. Minimum, typical and wider tiers define the range of phenomena and task contexts for each descriptor.
subject: Digital Technologies

generation_rules.notes: K-strand descriptors use phenomena_contexts. P-strand descriptor uses task_contexts. AC9TDIFP01 has some thin width at Foundation — the concept is narrow at this level. First Nations elaborations present in AC9TDIFK01.

width_notes.minimum: The narrowest context or task that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. Every student in the class meets this floor before the class moves on.
width_notes.typical: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects sound standard practice for the band.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena or task contexts, not difficulty. Each item is a concrete direction for advancing students. First Nations elaborations included as default wider directions where ACARA provides them.

AC9TDIFK01.minimum_width: Recognise and name at least two familiar digital systems; explore one digital system and describe what it does for a purpose.
AC9TDIFK01.typical_width: Recognise multiple digital systems across home and school contexts; explore what different systems do for different purposes; participate in a class activity using a digital system purposefully (e.g. video conference with an expert).
wider: Record audio or video of local community members' stories (with permission) to share in class — explore the digital system used for recording and discuss its purpose

Take photos (with permission) of First Nations Australians' material culture such as woven mats or baskets revealing intricate detail — explore the camera as a digital system and discuss what the photos are for and who they are shared with
Make a model of a digital system using cardboard boxes with a keyboard, screen and app icons — describe its features in a role-play scenario
elaborations: recognising digital systems that they interact with at home and school, for example smartphone, laptop or programmable toy
playing with (with guidance) and using different digital systems to explore what they do for a purpose, for example the class speaking to an expert via videoconference
recording, with permission, audio or video of local community members' stories to share in class, for example sharing cultural stories of First Nations Australians
taking photos, with permission, to share with others, for example close-up photos of First Nations Australians' material culture, such as woven mats or baskets revealing intricate detail
making a model of a digital system, using it in a role-play scenario and describing its features, for example a cardboard box with a keyboard and screen with app icons

AC9TDIFK02.minimum_width: Use a picture or object to represent one piece of data; identify one symbol and explain what it represents.
AC9TDIFK02.typical_width: Represent data about multiple people or things using pictures and objects across at least two contexts; identify multiple symbols and explain what each represents; begin to distinguish the symbol from the data itself.
wider: Examine the symbols and colours on the Australian Aboriginal flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag — identify what each element represents and discuss why symbols are used to represent important ideas
Compare an app icon on a screen with what the app does — explain that the icon is a symbol representing the app, not the app itself
Use coloured blocks to represent an attribute of the class (e.g. sports houses) — explain what each colour stands for and why different colours represent different groups
elaborations: drawing a picture representing each of their family members and their interests, for example drawing one family member with a surfboard and another with a skateboard
using coloured blocks to represent an attribute of people, for example representing students and their sports houses with different coloured blocks
using a symbol to represent an idea, but knowing that the symbol is not the data itself, for example the symbols and colour on both the Australian Aboriginal flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag

AC9TDIFP01.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of personal data and state that it belongs to them; sort one example into personal and one into public.
AC9TDIFP01.typical_width: Identify multiple examples of personal and public data; distinguish personal from public across familiar contexts; explain that personal data is owned by them and treated differently from public data.
wider: Identify where personal data could be made visible through digital systems — for example photos on a parent's or carer's social media, or a username shown to others in an online game; discuss why this matters
Compare a photo of themselves with their family (personal/private) with a photo of a local community site (public) — explain the difference and why each is treated differently

Limited width — at Foundation, the concept of personal vs public data is intentionally narrow. The genuine extension is connecting personal data to digital visibility and ownership, which is more fully addressed at Years 1-2 (AC9TDI2P05, AC9TDI2P07).
elaborations: listing things that contain personal and public data, for example photos of themselves with their family (private) and photos of local community sites (public)

identifying apps and websites they use where their personal data could be made visible, for example photos of themselves on parents' or carers' social media, or their username being shown to others in online games
